title: Divide and Conquer DP
html:
Divide and Conquer is a dynamic programming optimization.

Preconditions

Some dynamic programming problems have a recurrence of this form:

dp(i,j)=min⁡0≤k≤jdp(i−1,k−1)+C(k,j)dp(i, j) = \min_{0 \leq k \leq j} \\{ dp(i - 1, k - 1) + C(k, j) \\}dp(i,j)=0≤k≤jmin​dp(i−1,k−1)+C(k,j)

where C(k,j)C(k, j)C(k,j) is a cost function and dp(i,j)=0dp(i, j) = 0dp(i,j)=0 when j<0j \lt 0j<0.

Say 0≤i<m0 \leq i \lt m0≤i<m and 0≤j<n0 \leq j \lt n0≤j<n, and evaluating CCC takes O(1)O(1)O(1) time. Then the straightforward evaluation of the above recurrence is O(mn2)O(m n^2)O(mn2). There are m×nm \times nm×n states, and nnn transitions for each state.

Let opt(i,j)opt(i, j)opt(i,j) be the value of kkk that minimizes the above expression. Assuming that the cost function satisfies the quadrangle inequality, we can show that opt(i,j)≤opt(i,j+1)opt(i, j) \leq opt(i, j + 1)opt(i,j)≤opt(i,j+1) for all i,ji, ji,j. This is known as the monotonicity condition. Then, we can apply divide and conquer DP. The optimal "splitting point" for a fixed iii increases as jjj increases.

This lets us solve for all states more efficiently. Say we compute opt(i,j)opt(i, j)opt(i,j) for some fixed iii and jjj. Then for any j′<jj' < jj′<j we know that opt(i,j′)≤opt(i,j)opt(i, j') \leq opt(i, j)opt(i,j′)≤opt(i,j). This means when computing opt(i,j′)opt(i, j')opt(i,j′), we don't have to consider as many splitting points!

To minimize the runtime, we apply the idea behind divide and conquer. First, compute opt(i,n/2)opt(i, n / 2)opt(i,n/2). Then, compute opt(i,n/4)opt(i, n / 4)opt(i,n/4), knowing that it is less than or equal to opt(i,n/2)opt(i, n / 2)opt(i,n/2) and opt(i,3n/4)opt(i, 3 n / 4)opt(i,3n/4) knowing that it is greater than or equal to opt(i,n/2)opt(i, n / 2)opt(i,n/2). By recursively keeping track of the lower and upper bounds on optoptopt, we reach a O(mnlog⁡n)O(m n \log n)O(mnlogn) runtime. Refer to the code below for implementation details.

To prove the complexity of the divide and conquer, first note that there are O(log⁡n)O(\log{n})O(logn) levels in the recursion. We claim that O(n)O(n)O(n) steps are being done at each level. Let the total length of the opt\text{opt}opt intervals (denoted by optloptloptl and optroptroptr in the code) in the kkkth level be SkS_kSk​, and observe that any time an interval from level kkk of length xxx is split, the resulting interval(s) have total length at most x+1x + 1x+1. Furthermore, at level kkk, at most 2k2^k2k splits are performed, so we have that Sk+1≤Sk+2kS_{k + 1} \leq S_k + 2^kSk+1​≤Sk​+2k. Applying the bound inductively with S0=nS_0 = nS0​=n gives that for each level kkk,

Sk<n+2k∈O(n).S_k < n + 2^k \in O(n).Sk​<n+2k∈O(n).

Thus, the complexity of each divide and conquer is O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log{n})O(nlogn), and the complexity of the entire DP computation is O(mnlog⁡n)O(mn\log{n})O(mnlogn).

Generic implementation

Even though implementation varies based on problem, here's a fairly generic template. The function compute computes one row iii of states dp_cur, given the previous row i−1i-1i−1 of states dp_before. It has to be called with compute(0, n-1, 0, n-1). The function solve computes m rows and returns the result.

int m, n;
vector<long long> dp_before, dp_cur;

long long C(int i, int j);

// compute dp_cur[l], ... dp_cur[r] (inclusive)
void compute(int l, int r, int optl, int optr) {
    if (l > r)
        return;

    int mid = (l + r) >> 1;
    pair<long long, int> best = {LLONG_MAX, -1};

    for (int k = optl; k <= min(mid, optr); k++) {
        best = min(best, {(k ? dp_before[k - 1] : 0) + C(k, mid), k});
    }

    dp_cur[mid] = best.first;
    int opt = best.second;

    compute(l, mid - 1, optl, opt);
    compute(mid + 1, r, opt, optr);
}

long long solve() {
    dp_before.assign(n,0);
    dp_cur.assign(n,0);

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        dp_before[i] = C(0, i);

    for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
        compute(0, n - 1, 0, n - 1);
        dp_before = dp_cur;
    }

    return dp_before[n - 1];
}

Things to look out for

The greatest difficulty with Divide and Conquer DP problems is proving the monotonicity of optoptopt. One special case where this is true is when the cost function satisfies the quadrangle inequality, i.e., C(a,c)+C(b,d)≤C(a,d)+C(b,c)C(a, c) + C(b, d) \leq C(a, d) + C(b, c)C(a,c)+C(b,d)≤C(a,d)+C(b,c) for all a≤b≤c≤da \leq b \leq c \leq da≤b≤c≤d. Many Divide and Conquer DP problems can also be solved with the Convex Hull trick or vice-versa. It is useful to know and understand both!
